headline: High risk of shared-repo write conflicts and output-to-input cascading errors; prompt-injection and compliance risks are lower but present.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider has no clipboard or MCP bridge, so direct injection paths are limited. CrewAI can ingest developer-defined tool outputs and shared memory, and Aider can read/write repo files. The main pathway is manual or file-based content being treated as instructions, which is possible but not default and has small blast radius.
conditions: IF CrewAI is configured to read Aider-authored files as instructions without provenance checks, injection risk increases.
IF the shared repo is used as an instruction channel, attacker-controlled text can steer downstream actions.
mitigations: Separate instruction files from code files in the shared repo.
Add a short provenance header to any file passed between agents.
Require CrewAI to ignore comments or free-form text unless explicitly requested.
Review any Aider-generated markdown or prompts before CrewAI consumes them.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider touches source code and git history in a shared git repo, while CrewAI reads the host process working directory and can send data to model providers and configured tools. That creates a default shared-workspace leakage path for code or secrets present in the repo, even though neither profile shows clipboard or browser exfiltration.
conditions: IF sensitive files are present in the shared repository, both agents can access them.
IF CrewAI is configured with external model providers, file contents may leave the host process.
mitigations: Remove secrets from the shared repo before running either agent.
Use a separate repo or worktree per agent.
Disable or restrict CrewAI tools that transmit file contents externally.
Add .gitignore rules for sensitive artifacts and verify them in 1 minute.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider can write the filesystem and modify git state; CrewAI can also write the filesystem and read the same working directory. Because Aider shares state via a shared git repo and CrewAI has no default isolation, concurrent edits can collide and corrupt work or commits. This is a default-dangerous overlap with irreversible repo history impact.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout, concurrent writes can conflict.
IF CrewAI writes files while Aider auto-commits, commit history can diverge or be overwritten.
mitigations: Run each agent in a separate worktree.
Serialize write access with a simple lock file.
Assign one agent read-only access to the repo.
Pause one agent before the other makes commits.

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI’s role-playing crew and shared memory make it plausible that it will treat Aider’s outputs as authoritative inputs, while Aider can generate code changes that CrewAI may then act on. With no documented verification boundary between them, errors can cascade from generated text into downstream actions or commits.
conditions: IF CrewAI consumes Aider-generated patches or summaries without verification, mistakes propagate.
IF CrewAI uses Aider output to trigger tools or tasks, downstream actions can be wrong.
mitigations: Require a human review step before any action based on Aider output.
Have CrewAI validate diffs against tests before acting.
Limit Aider output to patch hunks, not free-form instructions.
Add a checklist that confirms each Aider claim against the repo.

E_compliance.rationale: Aider explicitly handles model-provider API keys and git history, while CrewAI handles developer-passed crew data and tool integrations. If regulated or sensitive data is placed in the shared workspace, retention and third-party processing obligations can diverge across the two systems. The profiles do not show a specific residency mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared repo or crew inputs, both agents may process it.
IF external model providers are enabled, retention and transfer terms may differ across agents.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace.
Document which provider processes each data class.
Turn off external providers for sensitive runs.
Add a quick retention review before enabling either agent on regulated data.
